nameStory: Staurodesmus incus gets its species name 'incus' from the Latin word for anvil, referring to the distinctive anvil-like shape of this tiny single-celled organism when viewed under a microscope. The genus name Staurodesmus means 'cross-shaped chain,' describing how these microscopic algae often link together in star-like formations.
description: Staurodesmus incus is a microscopic single-celled green alga that lives in freshwater environments throughout New England. Each individual cell is incredibly tiny - only about 20-30 micrometers across (that's smaller than the width of a human hair!). Under a microscope, the cells appear symmetrical with a distinctive constricted middle and often have small spines or projections extending outward, giving them their characteristic anvil-like appearance. You'll never see these with the naked eye, but they're important members of the plankton community in ponds and lakes.

idTips.label: Anvil Shape
idTips.description: Under high magnification, the cell has a distinctive anvil or dumbbell shape with a narrow constriction in the middle and broader ends

idTips.label: Cell Size
idTips.description: Extremely small at 20-30 micrometers - requires at least 400x magnification to see clearly

idTips.label: Symmetry
idTips.description: Perfectly symmetrical when viewed from above, with each half being an exact mirror image of the other

idTips.label: Green Color
idTips.description: Bright green due to chlorophyll, though may appear yellowish-green depending on lighting and microscope settings

idTips.label: Surface Texture
idTips.description: Cell wall appears smooth and glassy under high magnification, without the rough texture of some related species

habitat: Found in clean, soft-water ponds, lakes, and slow-moving streams throughout New England's forested regions. Prefers slightly acidic water with low mineral content, often in association with sphagnum moss bogs and mountain ponds. Most commonly found in the cooler waters of higher elevations and northern areas of the region.

seasonality.spring: Populations begin to grow as water temperatures warm and daylight hours increase. Best time to find them in temporary pools and newly ice-free ponds.
seasonality.summer: Peak abundance occurs during warm summer months when conditions are optimal for photosynthesis and reproduction.
seasonality.fall: Still present but populations may decline as temperatures cool and daylight decreases. Often found in deeper, more stable water bodies.
seasonality.winter: Present but dormant in ice-covered waters, with very low metabolic activity until spring thaw.

funFact: Despite being invisible to the naked eye, a single drop of pond water can contain hundreds of these microscopic organisms, each one capable of producing its own food through photosynthesis just like a tiny green plant - meaning you're literally looking at some of Earth's smallest solar-powered factories!
confusionNotes: Easily confused with other Staurodesmus species, which all share the basic anvil shape. The key is looking for the smooth cell wall and specific proportions - incus has a more pronounced waist and smoother outline than its spiny relatives.
contextualKnowledge: Though called an 'alga,' Staurodesmus belongs to a group that's more closely related to land plants than to seaweeds. These desmids (members of the Desmidiaceae family) are considered among the most beautiful microscopic organisms and have fascinated microscopists for over 150 years with their perfect geometric symmetry.
compareHints: Staurodesmus incus differs from its relatives by having a smoother outline and less pronounced spines compared to species like S. octocornis (which has eight distinct spines) or S. megacanthus (with much larger projections). The incus species has the most anvil-like proportions in the genus, with a particularly narrow waist relative to its end lobes.
